item.title: @SemiconductorsX：谷歌计划为其TPU直接采购HBM以降低成本，正与联发科及SK海力士展开合作
item.description:
Big tech is starting to buy HBM directly. Google is looking to cut out the middle layer for its TPU.

Asia Economic reported on the 28th that Google is pursuing direct HBM purchases for its Tensor Processing Unit. Digitimes said the company is exploring ways to source HBM without going through its existing partner Broadcom. Google is already working with MediaTek on next-generation TPU development. It is reviewing a split between semiconductor design and memory buying instead of handing both to Broadcom.
$GOOGL
The driver is rising AI infrastructure cost. Direct involvement lets Google negotiate price and supply terms with the manufacturers and skip intermediary fees. Counterpoint estimated that the current Broadcom model adds a 15-20% middle margin on HBM purchases. Bernstein analyzed cost differences for Google’s next AI chip. Assuming 6 million units of the 8th-generation TPU v8t, the MediaTek cooperation model comes to $8,434 per chip. That is roughly half the $16,996 figure under the Broadcom model.

HBM demand has been centered on Nvidia GPUs. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft are expanding their own AI chips and becoming new buyers. Google has said it has secured about 100 TPU customers. Oracle and others are looking to use Google’s AI semiconductors in their cloud services. Counterpoint projects HBM bit demand for AI server ASICs will rise 35 times from 2024 to 2028.
$SKHY
SK Hynix is known to have proposed joint design of custom HBM tailored to customer needs from the early stage of Google’s next TPU. Samsung is working with Broadcom, a major TPU development partner. The two signed an MOU in July covering HBM, foundry, and advanced packaging. From HBM4 onward, logic functions are integrated into the base die. Memory design matched to the customer’s accelerator structure becomes more important. Optimizing bandwidth, capacity, and power efficiency from the early stage of development is turning into a competitive factor.

Direct procurement can also be an opportunity for memory makers. Skipping the intermediary can lower procurement costs and raise price competitiveness. It can also increase direct cooperation with end customers as big tech expands its own AI semiconductor production. Some in the industry see limited impact on memory makers’ profitability or negotiation power. The cooperative relationship with manufacturers does not change simply because the customer gets involved in purchasing. Supply methods already differ by customer. Some data-center operators take SSDs. Others buy NAND chips directly and build their own systems. AI semiconductor cooperation ranges from design to memory procurement, foundry, and packaging depending on the customer’s capability and strategy.

How much of the 15-20% middle margin disappears once Google locks in direct HBM deals for the TPU?

Chinese memory makers are building faster and cheaper than consensus models assume, and SK hynix, Samsung and $MU will pay for it in market share. YMTC's IPO filing shows it is already under way.

Kioxia fell as much as 15.9% on 25 November on a forecast of lower NAND prices in 2028. Goldman now has 2028 NAND prices down slightly more than 20%, and names supply growth led by Chinese makers as the reason.

YMTC, China's largest NAND maker, is aiming for a STAR Market listing as early as Q1 2027. Its parent's prospectus shows Q1 2026 revenue of RMB 47.0B and net profit of RMB 33.4B. That is a ~71% net margin, and more than double its profit for all of 2025, in one quarter.

It held 14% of NAND shipments in Q2, third behind Samsung and SK hynix. Its two Wuhan fabs run about 200,000 wafers a month. Phase 3, its third Wuhan fab, is due to produce by end-2026, two more fabs are planned, and the long-term target is about 500,000 wafers a month, some of it DRAM. Morgan Stanley expects YMTC to add about 100,000 wafers a month in each of 2027 and 2028, and CXMT to add the same in DRAM every year from 2026 to 2028.

We think the build will come faster and larger than that, for four reasons:

1) Speed. Phase 3 broke ground in September 2025, had tools going in before the building was finished, and is due to produce a year ahead of its original 2027 plan. We expect the next Chinese memory fabs to go from groundbreaking to output in about 9 to 12 months. A typical fab takes about two years.

2) Capital. Phase 3 is about half owned by a Hubei state fund, the parent is raising RMB 33B, and the IPO comes on top. We think no incumbent funds new fabs that cheaply.

3) Tools. More than half of Phase 3's tools come from Chinese equipment makers, which we think are cheaper and faster to buy from than US suppliers.

4) Lithography. The one tool China cannot make is ASML's DUV scanner, the machine that prints the chip patterns. According to C114, YMTC and CXMT have stockpiled enough of them, with spares, for about three years of expansion.

The incumbents are doing the opposite. SK hynix, Samsung and Micron are earning around 80% gross margins by holding back output growth and raising prices instead. YMTC and CXMT put record profits into new fabs. Every quarter the price stays this high pays for more Chinese capacity.

That ends in share loss at the big three and then a race to the bottom on price. Once Chinese supply catches up, the incumbents defend share by cutting price, and a maker earning a 71% net margin can cut a long way and still make money. Kioxia and $SNDK feel it first because they are almost pure NAND. CXMT is running the same play in DRAM, so the share loss reaches SK hynix, Samsung and Micron too.

YMTC's filing now puts numbers and dates on that call.

What to watch: Phase 3 output in early 2027, YMTC's IPO timetable, and NAND contract prices. TrendForce expects them to fall 0 to 5% in Q1 2027, with every product category turning down from Q2 2027.

Global DRAM bit supply is expected to grow strongly from 2026 through 2028 as makers add capacity and move to advanced nodes. If server shipment growth slows in 2028, shortages ease and contract prices fall across all categories starting in the first quarter of 2028.

In the bear case, server OEMs cut procurement further after demand revisions. That triggers inventory reductions across the chain. Neocloud investment falls and consolidation rises. BIS export controls become stricter.

Server shipment growth could decelerate as early as 2027. Conventional DRAM contract prices reverse and begin declining in the fourth quarter of 2027, with wider drops in 2028.

item.title: @convequity：投资者分析认为前沿AI模型在编程等可验证领域的进展将快于开放式办公任务
item.description:
Over the past two quarters Claude's gains have looked narrow to us. We suspect much of the best improvement came from hand-built specialist datasets in fields such as philosophy.

That fits a pattern. Frontier AI models improve fastest where an answer can be checked quickly, and that is why we expect office tasks to take longer to match coding.

In coding, a model writes code, runs the tests and learns from the failures. The test does the grading, so the lab needs fewer human experts. The model can run against the same verifier again and again.

Parts of math and science work the same way. Biology has measurable outcomes, but lab experiments are slow, so the feedback arrives slowly.

Office work, open-ended research and anything that needs taste give noisy or late signals. That explains why the labs focus on verifiable work.

Where judgment rules, a lab has to pay experts to put their judgment into the training data, and peak performance in a new field may still need costly expert data. That data keeps its value only while the experts' knowledge stays current.

Our own investment work shows how fast expert knowledge moves. Market regimes shift, new information arrives and crowded trades stop working. A dataset built for last quarter's regime can look stale this quarter. The data has to be refreshed as the task itself changes.

Our view is that frontier models will improve unevenly. We expect gains to keep coming fast in coding and the checkable parts of math and science, and slower in open-ended work. The thing to watch is how fast labs can capture fresh judgment from people who are still forming it.

item.title: @convequity：探讨AI模型稀疏化趋势与3D DRAM及SRAM的技术路线抉择
item.description:
Fractile is betting that AI models will keep getting sparser, and that 3D DRAM is the memory they will need. Yet the Claude models are leading the frontier with low sparsity and larger experts, which suggests SRAM may be the better path forward.

At the same compute per token, a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model that uses 1/128 of its experts per token needs about 20 times the memory of one that uses about 1/6.

A MoE model is divided into many experts, and each token uses only a share of them. That share is the sparsity. The smaller the share, the sparser the model.

Sparsity is set when the model is designed. Designers first decide how much compute each token should use, then what share of the experts each token draws on. The total size of the model follows from those two choices.

Take a model that uses about 30B parameters per token. At about 1/6 sparsity, each token uses one sixth of the experts, so the whole model is roughly 180B parameters. At 1/128, the same 30B per token implies a model closer to 4 trillion parameters. That is about 20 times more to store for the same compute per token.

Sparsity lets labs build far bigger, more knowledgeable models without raising the cost of each token.

Every expert still has to sit in memory, because any token might need any of them. Different tokens in a batch also call different experts, so the chip has to pull weights from many places at once. Today's memory cannot supply those weights fast enough.

That is the case made for 3D DRAM. The argument is that it supplies both the capacity and the bandwidth, which would allow models that use 1/128 to 1/256 of the experts per token instead of about 1/6.

Our view is that the success of the Claude models suggests lower sparsity with larger experts, running on TPUs, can perform better than sparser models. We think the claim that 3D DRAM beats SRAM by supporting higher sparsity is already breaking down. Models are evolving faster than chip designers expected.

The thing to watch is the sparsity the leading labs choose in their next models.

item.title: @convequity：分析预测2026年AI需求转向具身智能与本地部署
item.description:
Superhuman coding, math and research favor the very largest models this year, and we think the next sources of AI demand do not need the same frontier chips.

2026 is the year these tasks became the breakthrough in demand. The largest models need $NVDA's Rubin-class hardware. Rubin's memory bandwidth lets a model activate more parameters for every token it produces.

Coding also suits self-improvement because the results can be checked. A model runs the tests, sees at once what passed and what failed, and tries again.

A model that improves this way helps its lab build the next, better model, so a lead compounds. That makes lacking Rubin-class chips especially costly for China right now.

Demand moves, though. We see growth in three areas: embodied AI, meaning AI that runs robots and other machines; local deployment, where a model runs on the user's own hardware; and industrial uses. None of the three needs the same frontier accelerators, and China is strong in all three.

Chinese models already hold much of the capability-per-dollar frontier below the top tier. In some size brackets, such as the one Qwen3.8-27B competes in, they lead decisively, after years of hard technical work.

That is why we think the long run stays open, even if this year's coding and math cycle belongs to whoever has the biggest clusters.

item.title: @convequity：分析机构认为Fractile芯片在内存速度与容量指标上难以兼得
item.description:
We think Fractile is unlikely to deliver both the memory speed and the memory capacity it claims on the same chip.

Fractile's headline claim is about 25x the per-chip bandwidth of HBM-based GPUs and XPUs, while keeping the model in cheaper, larger-capacity DRAM instead of HBM.

Bandwidth is how fast data moves between the memory and the processor. Capacity is how much data the memory stores.

The two come from different parts of the design. Bandwidth comes from stacking DRAM directly on the logic die, the chip that does the computing. Capacity depends on how many DRAM dies are in that stack.

If Fractile stacks only 2 to 4 DRAM dies on the logic die, it cannot match HBM-based chips on capacity in a like-for-like comparison. A stack that short limits how much memory each chip holds.

d-Matrix's Raptor shows the trade in practice. Raptor has 32GB of 3D DRAM per card. HBM4 accelerators have 192 to 288GB. d-Matrix plans to make up the capacity at rack scale.

The exception is a fan-out architecture, which spreads memory sideways across the package rather than relying purely on stacked dies.

Our view is that with a stack of only 2 to 4 DRAM dies, Fractile cannot match HBM-based chips on capacity per chip. The two things to watch are how many DRAM dies Fractile stacks and whether it uses a fan-out design.

Deeper dive available at Convequity.

item.title: @convequity：专家数据成本与模型蒸馏技术对中美顶尖AI实验室竞争格局的影响分析
item.description:
We think expensive expert data explains part of the lead Anthropic's Opus and OpenAI's Astra hold over Chinese models. Distillation lets rivals copy some of that ability at a fraction of the cost, making the lead harder to defend.

Both labs pay top specialists for their knowledge and judgment, up to $500 for a single conversation. We see only one Chinese lab paying at that level, and the leading Chinese labs spend less.

In distillation, a weaker model learns from a stronger model's answers.

In our illustration, a lab pays experts $400 an hour for 10,000 hours. That is $4 million of training data.

The lab sells the resulting model at $40 per equivalent hour. It earns back the $4 million in gross revenue after 100,000 hours.

A rival then buys 10,000 hours of the model's output at the same $40 an hour. That costs $400,000, a tenth of the original cost, and the rival captures much of the same ability.

Chinese teams say this works on some tasks and does not yet produce a full copy.

A frontier lab can protect the edge by selling its best systems only to a small group of U.S. enterprises. Once those capabilities go on wider sale, distillation lets some of the knowledge leak out. The thing to watch is when each lab puts its best system on wider sale.

Our view is that the expensive first wave from proprietary labs pays for the breakthrough. A cheaper second wave, with Chinese models in it, then brings it to far more people.

item.title: @convequity：Convequity：超大规模云厂商投资回报率与企业价值倍数分析，估值修复空间较大
item.description:
ROIC / WACC vs EV / IC: Hyperscalers Marked Down Too Far. Neo-Clouds, Mostly Not.

Convequity's AI Bubble Barometer (ABBX) pairs two metrics on its Fundamentals tab:

ROIC / WACC Ratio: return on AI capital (ROIC) over the cost of that capital (WACC). Above 1x, the spending creates value.

EV / IC Multiple: enterprise value over invested capital, what the market pays per dollar of capital.

Our question: has EV / IC fallen more than ROIC / WACC justifies?

1. HYPERSCALERS ($MSFT $AMZN $GOOGL $META $ORCL $CRWV $SPCX)

- ROIC / WACC fell 6%, from 2.82x (2Q26 reading) to 2.65x (3Q26 reading, live since 13 Nov).
- EV / IC fell 24%, from 6.80x at the 9 Oct close to 5.15x at the 25 Nov close.

EV / IC fell about four times as much, with ROIC / WACC still at a respectable 2.65x.

Clearest case, Google: EV / IC fell from 6.35x to 4.59x over the same closes; its ROIC / WACC edged up from 2.31x (2Q26) to 2.32x (3Q26).

2. NEO-CLOUDS ($NBIS $IREN $APLD $CORZ $CIFR $BTDR)

- ROIC / WACC fell 20%, from 1.40x (2Q26) to 1.12x (3Q26).
- EV / IC fell 57%, from 3.18x at the 9 Oct close to 1.38x at the 25 Nov close.

EV / IC fell faster here too, but mostly for good reason: at 1.12x, ROIC / WACC barely clears 1x, and IREN, Cipher and Bitdeer are below it.

Here both metrics use the same balance-sheet capital, so levels compare directly: on 9 Oct the market paid 3.18x EV / IC for 1.40x ROIC / WACC; on 25 Nov, 1.38x for 1.12x. The growth premium has mostly gone.

3. ALL 13

- ROIC / WACC fell 2.5%, from 1.25x (2Q26) to 1.22x (3Q26).
- EV / IC fell 25%, from 6.75x at the 9 Oct close to 5.08x at the 25 Nov close.

Yes, but this is the hyperscaler answer: neo-clouds are 0.5% of the 13's enterprise value at the 25 Nov close.

What we're watching 🔍

Oracle, which we hold, reports its November quarter on 14 Dec; its figures here are still from the quarter ended 31 August.

What would change our view: a 4Q26 hyperscaler ROIC / WACC reading falling as fast as EV / IC has.

item.title: @convequity：分析称华为计划于2027年2月推出自主HBM并加速Ascend 960DT芯片
item.description:
HBM is not Huawei's bottleneck. Its own memory stack has twice the data pins of HBM4

Huawei will present its own HBM, the stacked memory that feeds AI chips, at the ISSCC chip-design conference on 16 February 2027. The draft programme lists 4,096 data pins, twice the 2,048 of HBM4, the current standard. Its five layers are joined by wafer-on-wafer hybrid bonding, which bonds copper directly to copper with no solder.

Many investors still believe HBM is Huawei's bottleneck. Chosun Ilbo reported in September that CXMT, the Chinese memory maker, is stuck at a yield of about 25% on HBM3, where SK hynix is above 90%. The Information reported in November that smuggled Korean HBM often ends up with Huawei's customers.

In our view CXMT's low yield on standard HBM3 is a nothing burger. Huawei does not need to follow the HBM standard. It builds its own stack, with a wider interface, fewer layers and its own controllers inside, and it has no need to smuggle HBM.

So we are not surprised that Huawei is speeding up its Ascend 960DT AI chip, now due in 1Q27 instead of 4Q27. Our estimate from published specs: the 960DT moves 9.6 TB/s in and out of memory for 4 PFLOPS of compute. Nvidia's ($NVDA) Rubin moves 22 TB/s for 35 PFLOPS. Each Huawei chip has far less compute, but per unit of compute it has about 3.8x Rubin's memory bandwidth. The gap in networking bandwidth is wider.

We wrote in September 2025: "by using custom HBM standard whilst NVDA only customize the base die of HBM4, Huawei is ahead."

Huawei's progress is also great news for BE Semiconductor ($BESI), the Dutch maker of hybrid bonding machines and one of our holdings. Investors sold BESI this year because the HBM makers put hybrid bonding off and stayed on solder. It closed on 24 November 56% below its June high. Huawei's ISSCC papers put hybrid bonding in both memory and logic. If chipmakers outside China stay on solder, Huawei will outcompete them in both, so we expect them to adopt it. Seoul Economic Daily reported on 20 November that SK hynix plans to order BESI's hybrid bonders. We bought the dip in October.
